summary: Describes a Transport Model that carries SNMP over the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol, giving encrypted and authenticated management traffic. It also defines MIB objects to monitor and manage this model.

plainLanguage.summary:
SNMP is the protocol a management program uses to read and change settings on a remote network device. SNMPv3 can protect that traffic, but it needs its own set of users and keys to manage.

This document says to run SNMP inside an SSH session instead. SSH already handles encryption, integrity and the authentication of both ends, and most organisations already have SSH keys in place. The result is a management channel that uses the same credentials administrators already use for a command line.

which ports does snmp over ssh use
why use ssh instead of usm for snmp
what is the snmp ssh subsystem
subtitle: Runs SNMP inside an SSH session, so management traffic gets SSH's authentication, encryption and integrity.

tldr.problem: SNMPv3 added security through the User-based Security Model, but that model needs its own user and key infrastructure. Operators have reported that having to deploy a second one is a reason not to deploy SNMPv3 at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Transport Model that carries SNMP inside an SSH session. The SSH client opens a transport connection, authenticates the server and the principal, requests a session channel, and starts the snmp subsystem on it. SNMP messages then travel inside that channel, and the authenticated SSH identity is mapped to the securityName used for access control.
tldr.outcome: SNMP traffic is encrypted, integrity checked and mutually authenticated by SSH, and existing SSH credentials and key infrastructure can be reused. The RFC also defines the SNMP-SSH-TM-MIB with counters for session activity, and rules for deployment, including that public key verification, confidentiality and integrity must not be turned off.

sections.title: The Secure Shell Transport Model
sections.content:
This memo describes a Transport Model for the Simple Network Management Protocol using the Secure Shell protocol of RFC 4251 within a Transport Subsystem. The Transport Model is referred to as the Secure Shell Transport Model, or SSHTM.

The memo also defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets. In particular, it defines objects for monitoring and managing the Secure Shell Transport Model for SNMP.

Understanding the SNMP architecture of RFC 3411 and its terminology is important, because it explains where the Transport Model sits in that architecture and how it interacts with the other subsystems. The model follows the framework described in RFC 3410, where managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, generally through SNMP, and defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information. The MIB module specified here is compliant to SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The document follows SNMP terminology rather than the terminology of other specifications. The words manager and agent are not used, because in the RFC 3411 architecture all SNMP entities can act as manager, agent or both; the application names command generator, command responder, notification originator, notification receiver and proxy forwarder are used instead. The preferred word for a user is principal, meaning the who on whose behalf services are provided or processing takes place.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP has a layered design, and this document adds one layer: the transport layer that carries the SNMP messages. That layer is SSH.

sections.title: Why Run SNMP over SSH
sections.content:
Version 3 of SNMP added security to the protocol. The User-based Security Model was designed to be independent of other existing security infrastructures, to ensure it could function when third-party authentication services were not available, such as in a broken network. As a result it uses a separate user and key-management infrastructure. Operators have reported that having to deploy another user and key-management infrastructure in order to use SNMPv3 is a reason for not deploying SNMPv3.

This memo describes a Transport Model that makes use of the existing and commonly deployed Secure Shell security infrastructure. It is designed to meet the security and operational needs of network administrators, maximize usability in operational environments to achieve high deployment success, and at the same time minimize implementation and deployment costs.

The document addresses the requirement for the SSH client to authenticate the SSH server and for the SSH server to authenticate the SSH client, and describes how SNMP can use the authenticated identities in authorization policies for data access, in a manner that is independent of any specific Access Control Model. It also addresses the requirement to use client-authentication and key-exchange methods that support different security infrastructures and provide different security properties, by using client authentication as described in the SSH Authentication Protocol.

The model should work with any of the ssh-userauth methods, including publickey, password, hostbased, none, keyboard-interactive, gssapi-with-mic, gssapi-keyex, gssapi and external-keyx. The use of the none authentication method is NOT RECOMMENDED. Local accounts may be supported through the publickey, hostbased or password methods, and the password method allows integration with a deployed password infrastructure, such as AAA servers using RADIUS. The model SHOULD be able to take advantage of future-defined ssh-userauth methods, such as those using X.509 certificate credentials.

Using the security services provided by Secure Shell is the approach commonly used for the CLI, and it is the approach being adopted for NETCONF. This memo describes a method for invoking and running the SNMP protocol within a Secure Shell session as an SSH Subsystem, using the SSH connection protocol over the SSH transport protocol and ssh-userauth for authentication.
sections.plainLanguage:
The reason for this document is deployment cost. SNMPv3's own security needs users and keys that the organisation may not already have, and having to build that second system is often the reason SNMPv3 is never deployed.

SSH is already deployed nearly everywhere, so reusing it removes that extra work. The price is that SNMP then runs inside SSH, and inherits SSH's rules about keys and authentication.

sections.title: How SSHTM Fits into the Transport Subsystem
sections.content:
A Transport Model is a component of the Transport Subsystem defined in RFC 5590, within the SNMP architecture. The SSH Transport Model fits between the underlying SSH transport layer and the Message Dispatcher. It establishes a channel between itself and the SSH Transport Model of another SNMP engine: the sending Transport Model passes unencrypted messages from the Dispatcher to SSH to be encrypted, and the receiving Transport Model accepts decrypted incoming messages from SSH and passes them to the Dispatcher. After an SSH Transport Model channel is established, SNMP messages can conceptually be sent through the channel from one SNMP Message Dispatcher to another, and multiple SNMP messages MAY pass through the same channel. The model performs the translation between SSH-specific security parameters and SNMP-specific, model-independent parameters.

For incoming messages, SSH-specific security parameters are translated by the Transport Model into security parameters independent of the Transport and Security Models. The model accepts messages from the SSH Subsystem, records the transport-related and SSH-security-related information, including the authenticated identity, in a cache referenced by tmStateReference, and passes the whole message and the tmStateReference to the Dispatcher using the receiveMessage() interface. For outgoing messages, the Transport Model takes input provided by the Dispatcher in the sendMessage() interface, converts it into suitable security parameters for SSH, establishes sessions as needed, and passes messages to the SSH Subsystem for sending.

SSH sessions are uniquely identified within the SSH Transport Model by the combination of tmTransportAddress and tmSecurityName associated with each session. Because naming policies might differ between administrative domains, many SSH client packages support a user@hostname:port addressing syntax that operators can use to align non-equivalent account names, and the SnmpSSHAddress Textual Convention mirrors this notation. When that notation is used, the SSH connection should be established with an SSH user name matching the user portion of the notation. If no user portion is specified, the tmSecurityName is used as the SSH user name. The SnmpSSHAddress and tmSecurityName associated with an SSH session MUST remain constant for the life of the session, and different SnmpSSHAddress values result in individual SSH sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: The model sits between the part of SNMP that dispatches messages and the SSH layer underneath. Its job is to hand unencrypted SNMP messages down to SSH, take decrypted ones back up, and translate between SSH's idea of who is on the other end and SNMP's idea of a security name.

sections.title: Threats Covered and the Security Level
sections.content:
The model provides protection against the threats identified by the RFC 3411 architecture. Against modification of information, SSH verifies that the contents of each message have not been modified during transmission by digitally signing each SSH packet. Against masquerade, SSH provides for verification of the identity of the SSH server through the transport protocol server authentication, and of the identity of the SSH client-side principal through the authentication protocol, using public key, password and host-based mechanisms. Verification of the client's identity matters because the SNMP Access Control Subsystem uses it to ensure that only authorized principals have access to sensitive data; the SSH user identity is provided to the Transport Model so it can be mapped to an SNMP model-independent securityName.

Against message stream modification, SSH protects against malicious reordering or replaying of messages within a single session by using sequence numbers and integrity checks, and against replay across sessions by generating fresh keys for each session. Against disclosure, SSH allows all traffic between SNMP engines to be encrypted.

The RFC 3411 architecture recognizes three levels of security: noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv and authPriv. SSH provides support for encryption and data integrity, and while it is technically possible to support no authentication and no encryption in SSH, that is NOT RECOMMENDED by the SSH transport specification.

The model determines from SSH the identity of the authenticated principal and the type and address associated with an incoming message, and provides this information to SSH for an outgoing message. The transport-layer algorithms used for authentication, data integrity and encryption SHOULD NOT be exposed to the Transport Model layer. The model has no mechanism by which it can test whether an underlying SSH connection provides authentication or privacy, so it trusts that the connection has been properly configured. An implementation MUST use an SSH connection that provides authentication, data integrity and encryption meeting the highest SNMP security level, authPriv. Outgoing messages specified with a securityLevel of noAuthNoPriv or authNoPriv are actually sent with authPriv-level protection.
sections.plainLanguage:
SSH covers the four threats the SNMP architecture names: someone altering a message, someone pretending to be the server or the client, someone replaying old messages, and someone reading the traffic. The model does not check any of this itself; it relies on the SSH connection having been set up correctly.

One consequence is worth stating plainly. Whatever the SNMP message asked for in terms of security level, the traffic is actually sent with the strongest protection, because there is no way for the model to tell SSH to do less.

sections.title: Establishing, Using and Closing a Session
sections.content:
For an incoming message the model queries the SSH engine, in an implementation-dependent manner, to determine the address the message came from, the user name authenticated by SSH and a session identifier. It then derives a tmTransportAddress: on the client side, the address used to establish the session, including any user@ prefix; on the server side, the address the first message came from, which MUST remain constant for the whole session. It derives a tmSecurityName the same way: on the client side, the value used to establish the session; on the server side, the SSH user name. It then creates a cache entry holding the transport domain snmpSSHDomain, the derived address and security name, the transport security level authPriv, and a session identifier that must uniquely identify the session and must not be reused until no references to it remain. The message and the cache reference are passed to the Dispatcher.

For an outgoing message the Dispatcher passes the destination domain, address, the message and a cache reference. If the reference does not point at a cache with the expected values, the model increments the snmpSshtmSessionInvalidCaches counter, discards the message and returns an error. It then looks for a session to use: a session matching the session identifier, address and security name is preferred; failing that, a session matching the address and security name; failing that, it calls openSession(). If openSession fails the message is discarded and the error is passed back; if it succeeds, the destination, address, security name and session identifier are recorded for later use when an incoming message arrives. The whole message is then passed to SSH for encapsulation as data in an SSH message over the identified session.

Establishing a session follows a fixed sequence. The session opens counter is incremented. The client establishes an SSH transport connection, authenticates the server and exchanges keys for message integrity and encryption; the transport address associated with a session MUST remain constant for its lifetime. The client then invokes an SSH authentication service to authenticate the principal. If the transport address contains a user name followed by an @ character, that name should be presented to the SSH server as the user name for authentication; otherwise the tmSecurityName is used. If user authentication fails, the connection is closed and the user-auth-failure counter is incremented. The client then invokes the ssh-connection service and requests a channel of type session, and then invokes snmp as an SSH Subsystem. If either step fails, the connection is closed and the corresponding counter is incremented. Finally the session identifier is set in the cache, and the security name used to establish the session must be the only one used with it.

Servers associated with SNMP entities using this model MUST default to providing access to the snmp SSH Subsystem if the SSH session is established using the IANA-assigned TCP ports 5161 and 5162, so that SNMP traffic can be easily identified and filtered by firewalls and other network devices. Servers SHOULD be configurable to allow access over other ports. Closing a session increments the closes counter, and, if a session with that identifier exists, asks SSH to close it.
sections.plainLanguage:
Setting up a session takes five steps: open the encrypted connection, authenticate the user, open a channel, start the SNMP subsystem on that channel, and record the session so later messages reuse it.

Incoming messages do not need any of that. The model asks SSH who sent the message and what user was authenticated, then hands the message and that information to the rest of SNMP.

sections.title: The MIB Module
sections.content:
The MIB module provides management of the Secure Shell Transport Model. It defines an OID to identify the SNMP-over-SSH transport domain, a Textual Convention for SSH addresses, and several statistics counters.

The snmpSSHDomain object identity is the SNMP-over-SSH transport domain, whose corresponding transport address is of type SnmpSSHAddress. An SNMP entity using the snmpSSHDomain Transport Model must be capable of accepting messages up to and including 8192 octets in size, and implementation of larger values is encouraged whenever possible. The securityName prefix to be associated with the domain is ssh, which may be used by Security Models or other components to identify which secure transport infrastructure authenticated a securityName.

The SnmpSSHAddress Textual Convention represents either a hostname or IP address, along with a port number and an optional user name. The address may begin with a user name followed by an @ character, which indicates the user name to use when authenticating to an SSH server; it must be encoded in UTF-8, and if missing, the SNMP securityName should be used. The hostname is always in US-ASCII, with internationalized hostnames encoded in US-ASCII as specified in RFC 3490, and it is followed by a colon and a decimal port number in US-ASCII. An IPv4 address must be in dotted decimal format followed by a colon and a decimal port number, and an IPv6 address must be in colon-separated format, surrounded by square brackets, followed by a colon and a decimal port number. Values of this convention might not be directly usable as transport-layer addressing information and may require runtime resolution, so applications that write them must be prepared for handling errors when such values are not supported or cannot be resolved.

The session group holds eight read-only counters of type Counter32: snmpSshtmSessionOpens, the number of times an openSession() request has been executed as an SSH client, whether it succeeded or failed; snmpSshtmSessionCloses, the same for closeSession(); snmpSshtmSessionOpenErrors, the number of times an openSession() request failed to open a transport connection or to authenticate the server; snmpSshtmSessionUserAuthFailures, the number of times an openSession() request failed due to user-authentication failures; snmpSshtmSessionNoChannels, the number of times it failed due to channel-open failures; snmpSshtmSessionNoSubsystems, the number of times it failed because it could not connect to the requested subsystem; snmpSshtmSessionNoSessions, the number of outgoing messages dropped because the same session was no longer available; and snmpSshtmSessionInvalidCaches, the number of outgoing messages dropped because the tmStateReference referred to an invalid cache.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB module gives the transport domain a name and an address format, and it adds eight counters. Between them the counters show how many sessions were opened and closed and where the failures came from: the transport connection, the user authentication, the channel, the subsystem, or a session that had already gone away.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The model will likely not work in conditions where remote access to the CLI has stopped working. It assumes that TCP and IP continue to operate correctly between the communicating nodes. Failures in either node, the death of the daemon serving the communication, routing problems, firewalls that block the traffic and other problems can all prevent it from working. In situations where management access has to be very reliable, operators should consider mitigating measures such as dedicated management-only networks, point-to-point links, and the ability to use alternate protocols and transports.

To have SNMP properly use the security services provided by SSH, the model MUST be used with a Security Model that knows how to process a tmStateReference, such as the Transport Security Model for SNMP. If the model is configured to use AAA services, operators should consider configuring support for local authentication mechanisms, such as local passwords, so SNMP can continue operating during times of network stress.

The SSH protocol has its own window mechanism, and there are noticeable bandwidth and processing overheads to handling window adjustment messages, which can be avoided by sending them less frequently. SSH also requires CPU-intensive calculations to establish a session key during session establishment, which means short-lived sessions become computationally expensive compared to the User-based Security Model, which has no notion of a session key. Other transport security protocols such as TLS support session resumption, allowing a cached session key to be reused; such a mechanism does not exist for SSH, so SNMP applications should keep SSH sessions for longer periods.

To initiate SSH connections, an entity must be configured with SSH client credentials plus information to authenticate the server. While hosts are often configured as SSH clients, most internetworking devices are not, so to send notifications over this model the device will need to be configured as an SSH client.
sections.plainLanguage:
Management traffic over SSH is only as reliable as SSH itself. If the network is in trouble, the AAA servers are unreachable or a firewall blocks the port, SNMP stops working, so operators are told to keep local credentials as a fallback and to consider a dedicated management network.

There is also a cost. Opening an SSH session involves expensive key calculations, so the model asks for long-lived sessions rather than a new one per message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The model relies on SSH mutual authentication, binding of keys, confidentiality and integrity, and any authentication method that meets the requirements of the SSH architecture will provide the properties of mutual authentication and binding of keys. SSHv2 provides perfect forward secrecy for encryption keys. The model has no way to verify that server authentication was performed, to learn the host's public key in advance, or to verify that the correct key is being used; it simply trusts that these are properly configured by the implementer and deployer.

SSH provides the none userauth method, and the model MUST NOT be used with an SSH connection using it. While SSH does support turning off confidentiality and integrity, they MUST NOT be turned off when used with this model.

Skipping public-key verification is also forbidden. For the common case of Diffie-Hellman signed by public keys, the client must know the host's public key in advance and verify that the correct key is used. If that step is skipped, authentication of the SSH server to the client is not done; confidentiality and integrity to the server still exist, but they are of dubious value when an attacker can insert himself between the client and the real SSH server. Some userauth methods may defend against this, but many common ones, including password and keyboard-interactive, do not and in fact depend on the server's identity having been verified. SSH MUST NOT be configured to skip public-key verification for use with this model, and MUST NOT be configured using the none MAC algorithm, since that effectively removes authentication.

Notifications are authorized to be sent to a receiver based on the securityName used by the notification originator's engine, and this authorization happens before the message is sent and before the credentials of the remote receiver have been verified. The credentials presented by a notification receiver MUST therefore match the expected values for a given transport address, and ownership of the credentials MUST be properly cryptographically verified.

On the MIB module: there are no management objects with a read-write or read-create access clause, so an intruder cannot alter or create them through a direct SNMP SET. Some of the readable objects may still be considered sensitive, since the information in the snmpSshtmSession group can reflect the configured capabilities of a remote SSH server, which could help an attacker. Deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED; instead it is RECOMMENDED to deploy SNMPv3 with cryptographic security enabled.
sections.plainLanguage:
The model has no security machinery of its own; everything rests on the SSH connection being configured properly. Three settings must not be weakened: the none authentication method must not be used, public key verification must not be skipped, and neither confidentiality nor integrity may be turned off.

Skipping key verification is the dangerous one. An attacker in the middle would then see the management traffic and could take the password used to log in.

layers.detail: Multiplexes the encrypted tunnel into channels

viz.caption: OPENING AN SNMP SESSION OVER SSH

messages.label: SSH TRANSPORT CONNECTION
messages.note: The client authenticates the server and exchanges keys for integrity and encryption.

messages.label: SSH USER AUTHENTICATION
messages.note: The client authenticates the principal, for example with a public key.

messages.label: SNMP SUBSYSTEM
messages.note: The snmp subsystem is started on the channel.

messages.label: SNMP MESSAGES
messages.note: Several SNMP messages may pass through the same channel.

items.label: Opens
items.desc: openSession() requests executed as an SSH client, whether they succeeded or failed.

items.label: Closes
items.desc: closeSession() requests executed as an SSH client, whether they succeeded or failed.

items.label: Open errors
items.desc: openSession() requests that failed to open a transport connection or to authenticate the server.

items.label: User auth failures
items.desc: openSession() requests that failed because of user authentication.

items.label: No channels
items.desc: openSession() requests that failed to open a channel.

items.label: No subsystems
items.desc: openSession() requests that could not connect to the requested subsystem.

items.label: No sessions
items.desc: Outgoing messages dropped because the same session was no longer available.

items.label: Invalid caches
items.desc: Outgoing messages dropped because the tmStateReference referred to an invalid cache.
